tldr: This paper presents NeoRacer, an open-source 1:12 scale autonomous race car that packs research-grade AI compute (67 TOPS) and precision sensors into a pre-assembled vehicle for around $2,700.
hero_caption: The three pillars of NeoRacer (production and scaling, research translation, and education and competition) along with its physical (REAL) and simulated (SIM) co-development model. A tight feedback loop connects the manufacturer, university labs, and the community.
overview:
Standard benchmark datasets have long driven reproducible progress in machine learning, but autonomous systems robotics—and autonomous racing in particular—still sorely lacks widely accepted standard hardware. Researchers have had to choose between assembling one-off custom cars or purchasing niche commercial platforms costing $4,000 to $6,000. This fragmentation makes it nearly impossible to fairly benchmark algorithms or reproduce results across institutions. Meanwhile, budget educational robotics kits provide under a few TOPS of compute, falling far short of running modern LiDAR SLAM and real-time deep learning inference side by side.

To bridge this divide, the authors co-developed NeoRacer with the Neobotics Foundation and Seeed Studio. It is an open-source, standardized 1:12 scale racing platform built around an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano with 67 TOPS of AI compute. It comes equipped with a 270° LiDAR, a 120 fps global-shutter camera, a 9-axis IMU, and a high-resolution motor encoder. Pre-assembled and driver-configured, NeoRacer costs roughly $2,700—less than half the price of existing pre-assembled alternatives (such as complete F1Tenth-style cars near $6,000) while offering more than three times the compute.

Insights gained from a fast-paced pilot deployment at MIT (15 undergraduates over two weeks) directly drove key hardware refinements, such as switching from a 30 fps to a 120 fps camera to eliminate perceptual lag at racing speeds and redesigning the power distribution board to handle thermal loads. In addition, the team built Neobotics Playground, a browser-based 3D simulator sharing the exact same Python API as the real car, and introduced a 3-identifier release scheme to strictly trace hardware revisions and production batches. The result is a highly reproducible research and education platform where teams compete purely on algorithmic merit, not hardware discrepancies.
contributions: Packaged a 67 TOPS Jetson Orin Nano and a full sensor suite into a pre-assembled car for around $2,700, drastically lowering the barrier to entry for research-grade autonomous racing.
Decoupled the real-time control pipeline onto a dedicated ESP32-S3 microcontroller board (OSCORE), ensuring deterministic actuation and robust fail-safes regardless of compute load on the Linux host.
Built Neobotics Playground, a browser-based 3D simulator featuring an identical Python API to the physical car, enabling zero-barrier competition qualifiers and seamless Sim-to-Real transfer.
Established a Three-Identifier Release Scheme that ties hardware revisions, software stacks, and manufacturing batches into a single string for strict cross-institution experimental reproducibility.

sections.heading: Why does autonomous racing urgently need shared standard hardware?
sections.summary: Autonomous driving education and research are polarized between underpowered budget toys and prohibitively expensive research cars. NeoRacer fills this gap with an affordable, high-compute, pre-assembled standard platform.
sections.details:
Autonomous driving is an integrative discipline spanning perception, planning, control, machine learning, and real-time systems. Yet hardware platforms in academia remain sharply polarized. Sub-$1,000 educational kits like DuckieBot or PiCar-X offer less than 1 TOPS of compute, making it impossible to run modern deep-learning perception alongside dense SLAM. On the other end, full-featured research platforms like F1Tenth or MuSHR demand around $3,800 in parts alone, and turnkey builds (such as RACECAR/J) easily reach $6,000.

This division leads to three major bottlenecks. First, budget-constrained schools and labs are locked out of hands-on autonomous systems research. Second, even well-funded labs spend weeks sourcing parts from dozens of vendors, custom-machining chassis plates, and debugging low-level drivers before any research begins. Third, because every car has slightly different hardware specs, it is impossible to run a truly fair benchmark comparing which algorithm performs best.

NeoRacer tackles all three issues head-on. By partnering with Seeed Studio for industrial-scale manufacturing, it ships pre-assembled for about $2,700 with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (67 TOPS), a 270° LiDAR, a 120 fps global-shutter camera, and a 9-axis IMU. Out of the box, it can execute LiDAR SLAM, deep-learning inference, and a 30 Hz real-time control loop simultaneously, all while remaining fully compliant with official F1Tenth rules.

sections.heading: How does NeoRacer stand out from F1Tenth and low-cost robots?
sections.summary: While F1Tenth pioneered 1:10 scale racing, its high cost, multi-vendor sourcing, and build effort remain barriers. Low-cost educational robots lack Ackermann steering and adequate compute. NeoRacer uniquely bridges these worlds.
sections.details:
A survey of small-scale autonomous platforms reveals several distinct approaches:

- **F1Tenth**: The pioneer of 1:10 scale autonomous racing. It features serious hardware like the Jetson Xavier NX (21 TOPS) and a Hokuyo LiDAR (UST-10LX, ~$1,200 alone), but the bill of materials (BOM) tops $3,800, and assembled versions run close to $6,000. Parts span over a dozen suppliers, meaning post-crash repairs often take weeks of re-ordering and custom fabrication. Furthermore, well-funded teams frequently upgrade to premium LiDARs (like the Hokuyo UTM-30LX-EW, ~$4,375) or Jetson Orin NX modules, fueling an unwanted hardware arms race.
- **MIT RACECAR & MuSHR**: MIT's RACECAR broke ground in education, but its original hardware has aged. Its successor, RACECAR Neo, combines a Raspberry Pi 4 with a Google Coral Edge TPU, but compute constraints prevent it from running SLAM and deep learning concurrently, not to mention component shortages. The University of Washington's MuSHR platform faces similar hurdles with cost and availability at scale.
- **Low-cost educational robots**: Platforms like DuckieBot (~$1,098 assembled, Jetson Nano 0.5 TOPS) and TurtleBot4 (~$1,850, Raspberry Pi 4) are budget-friendly, but rely on differential-drive steering. NeoRacer, by contrast, uses Ackermann front-wheel steering matching real passenger cars. This makes it ideal for teaching vehicle dynamics, slip angles, and aggressive high-speed cornering control.

NeoRacer stands alone as the only pre-assembled platform under $3,000 that pairs authentic Ackermann kinematics with 67 TOPS of research-grade AI compute.

sections.heading: No-compromise hardware: Compute, perception, and chassis details
sections.summary: Centered around a Jetson Orin Nano, NeoRacer integrates a 270° LiDAR, a 120 fps global-shutter camera, and an ESP32-S3-powered real-time board (OSCORE) onto a durable 1:12 chassis built for safety and easy maintenance.
sections.details:
NeoRacer measures 380 mm long, 300 mm wide, 220 mm tall, and weighs under 3 kg. Its architecture is organized into five core subsystems:

- **Compute module (3.1)**: Uses an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano mounted on a Seeed Studio J401 carrier board. With an Ampere-architecture GPU delivering 67 TOPS of AI performance, 8 GB of LPDDR5 RAM, and a 128 GB NVMe SSD, it comes pre-installed with JetPack 6.2 (Ubuntu Linux, CUDA 12.x, TensorRT, and ROS2). It effortlessly runs Cartographer LiDAR SLAM, YOLOv8 object detection, and path tracking in parallel at 30 Hz.
- **Perception suite (3.2)**: Features a Richbeam LakiBeam1 horizontal 270° LiDAR with a 25 m range (10–30 Hz scan rate, 0.08°–0.24° angular resolution). The vision sensor is a 2.3 MP global-shutter camera capable of 120 fps at 1280×720 resolution in racing mode. Free from rolling-shutter jelly distortion, it provides crisp lane detection and AprilTag tracking even past 20 km/h (~6 m/s). An onboard 9-axis IMU and a high-resolution motor encoder (up to 4096 counts/rev) fill the dead-reckoning gap between LiDAR scans.
- **Drivetrain and actuators (3.3)**: A central shaft-driven 4WD system powered by a brushed DC motor (11,000 RPM free-run) drives all four wheels. Steering is actuated by a high-torque 20 kg waterproof metal-gear servo. Four-wheel independent aluminum coil-over suspension, all-terrain tires, and a rugged front bumper ensure the car withstands high-speed wall collisions.
- **Embedded control board (OSCORE) (3.4)**: A custom board powered by a dual-core 240 MHz ESP32-S3 microcontroller. It fully isolates the hard real-time domain—generating PWM for steering and ESC, decoding quadrature encoders, and executing fail-safes—so that spikes in Linux compute load never cause actuation jitter. A single USB 2.0 cable connects OSCORE to the Jetson, and an onboard USB hub (CH339F) bridges LiDAR Ethernet and IMU data to the host. A hardware watchdog brings the car to a safe stop if host communication drops.
- **Power, networking, and safety (3.5–3.7)**: A single 3S LiPo battery (11.1 V, 5200 mAh / 50C recommended) powers the car through regulators delivering 19 V to the Jetson and dedicated 5 V rails to sensors. An onboard Wi-Fi 6 travel router provides an isolated local network, enabling seamless SSH and ROS2 topic streaming even under strict campus IT policies. A 2.4 GHz remote transmitter provides an instant physical kill switch and a 15% low-speed training mode.

sections.heading: Protecting reproducibility: Tracking hardware, software, and production runs
sections.summary: To prevent the hardware drift that often plagues open-source hardware, NeoRacer assigns three identifiers—hardware revision, software release, and a manufacturing batch hash—to guarantee exact cross-lab traceability.
sections.details:
When multiple research labs deploy open-source hardware as a common experimental platform, the biggest threat to reproducibility is hardware drift—subtle component substitutions over time that silently break code. NeoRacer addresses this by tagging every vehicle with a Three-Identifier Release Scheme:

- **Hardware revision (e.g., NR-HW-v2.1)**: Defines the physical design, mounting footprints, sensor models, and connector pinouts.
- **Software release (e.g., nrlib-v3.4)**: References a locked, validated bundle containing the OS image, ROS2 packages, device drivers, and simulation assets.
- **Manufacturing run (e.g., MFG-2026-W18-seeed-a1f3e2)**: Encodes the production year, ISO week number, contract manufacturer, and git hashes of the BOM and firmware.

By citing a single string like `NR-HW-v2.1 / nrlib-v3.4 / MFG-2026-W18-seeed-a1f3e2` in a publication, researchers anywhere in the world can identify and replicate the exact experimental setup.

Production follows a four-stage lifecycle: Freeze, Batch build, Validation, and Community feedback. When users order spare parts, referencing this ID guarantees they receive drop-in compatible replacements.

sections.heading: Software architecture: Seamless bridge from ROS2 to browser simulation
sections.summary: Built on JetPack 6.2 and ROS2 with pre-configured drivers, NeoRacer shares an identical Python API between its browser-based Playground simulator and the physical vehicle. Code written in the browser runs directly on track.
sections.details:
NeoRacer's software stack is engineered to let users go from unboxing to writing autonomous control code in minutes.

- **ROS2 and pre-configured drivers (5.1–5.3)**: Built on Ubuntu via JetPack 6.2 with ROS2 installed out of the box. LiDAR scans, camera frames, IMU readings, odometry, and RC transmitter inputs are exposed through standard ROS2 topics, and actuator targets are received via standard drive messages. Standard navigation stacks like Nav2, Cartographer, and SLAM Toolbox work without modification, and TensorRT-optimized YOLOv8 inference runs alongside LiDAR SLAM with compute to spare.
- **Stable API via racecar-neo-library (5.4)**: A high-level Python library serves as the primary programming interface for students and researchers. Inherited from the MIT RACECAR project, this abstraction ensures that user-level control algorithms remain unchanged even if future batches update sensor models or pinouts.
- **Neobotics Playground (5.5)**: The centerpiece of the software environment is a fully browser-based 3D simulator. The split interface displays a Python code editor on the left, live sensor plots in the center, and a 3D track view with a ghost car showing the best lap on the right. Crucially, Playground uses the exact same library calls and API as the real car. Once an algorithm completes laps in the browser, the exact code can be pushed to the physical car without edits. For advanced reinforcement learning and robotics research, official URDF models and bridge nodes are also provided for MuJoCo, Isaac Lab, and Gazebo.

sections.heading: Research enablement: Reinforcement learning, safety verification, and SoC resources
sections.summary: Far more than an educational kit, NeoRacer is a testbed for cutting-edge robotics research. It enables Sim-to-Real reinforcement learning, Lyapunov-certified neural control, and real-time SoC memory contention analysis.
sections.details:
NeoRacer provides an out-of-the-box experimental platform for several active research domains:

- **Learning-based control on embedded hardware and Sim-to-Real**: Racing policies trained with reinforcement learning often fail on real hardware due to unmodeled latency and actuator non-linearities. Thanks to its kinematically matched simulator and deterministic ESP32 control path, NeoRacer allows fair benchmarking of Sim-to-Real techniques (such as RE+AL or CAPS) and fulfillment priority logic.
- **Stability-certified neural control**: For safety-critical learning control using neural Lyapunov functions or barrier certificates, researchers can test whether theoretical safety envelopes proved in simulation hold under extreme physical driving conditions.
- **Real-time resource management on heterogeneous SoCs**: Modern autonomous pipelines see SLAM, deep-learning models, and motion planners competing for CPU, GPU, and memory bus bandwidth. NeoRacer enables researchers to quantify how memory contention spikes translate into real physical lap times and tracking drift on track, rather than relying solely on synthetic benchmarks.
- **Hardware/software co-design**: With its modular carrier board interface, the compute unit can be swapped for FPGA-plus-CPU architectures. This makes it possible to study offloading real-time control logic into programmable fabric and compare the results directly against the Orin Nano baseline.

sections.heading: Reference curriculum: A 12-week journey from browser to track
sections.summary: A 12-week university course model designed for 48 students in 12 teams. Assignments and progress tracking are baked directly into the Playground simulator, requiring only introductory Python as a prerequisite.
sections.details:
NeoRacer includes a comprehensive 12-week, 4-credit reference syllabus structured around two 75-minute lectures and one 50-minute lab each week.

The target class size is 48 students divided into 12 four-person teams. The only prerequisite is introductory Python programming, allowing robotics beginners to progress steadily through foundational autonomous vehicle concepts.

Assignments and labs are delivered as structured 'gate challenges' directly within the Neobotics Playground browser simulator. Students first implement wall-following and obstacle-avoidance controllers in simulation; once validated, they deploy the identical script onto physical cars on track. Grading is based on weekly pass/fail gate milestones (40%), an autonomous simulation midterm demo (20%), a final physical autonomous racing project (30%), and class participation (10%). Gamified mechanics award experience points (XP) for fastest lap times, clean coding practices, and peer support.

sections.heading: Cost analysis: How does it compare to $6,000 commercial platforms?
sections.summary: Priced at $2,700 retail and dropping to $2,200 for institutional bulk orders of 15+ units. A $26,400 lab budget that could only buy 4 turnkey F1Tenth cars can fully outfit 12 NeoRacer teams.
sections.details:
NeoRacer retails for $2,699, with an early-bird pre-order price of $2,499 and an institutional bulk discount of $2,200 per unit for orders of 15 or more.

Consider a representative university lab startup budget of $26,400. Sourcing turnkey F1Tenth platforms (such as RACECAR/J at ~$6,000 each) yields only four vehicles, forcing most students to watch from the sidelines. Conversely, while low-cost DuckieBots (0.5 TOPS) would permit 24 units, their limited compute cannot support high-speed SLAM and perception pipelines. With NeoRacer's bulk pricing, that same $26,400 budget purchases 12 fully assembled vehicles—equipping an entire 48-student class with one car per 4-person team.

To further broaden access for underfunded institutions, a 501(c)(3) non-profit 'Sponsor-a-Kit' initiative allows corporate or individual sponsors to donate complete cars for $3,200, which includes international freight, spare parts, and setup support.

sections.heading: Field testing at MIT: Lessons learned and hardware improvements
sections.summary: During a rigorous two-week pilot with 15 students at MIT, heavy continuous racing revealed power board overheating and camera frame rate limits at 6 m/s. The team quickly upgraded to a redesigned power board and a 120 fps camera.
sections.details:
NeoRacer's design was battle-tested during MIT's Independent Activities Period (IAP), an intensive two-week winter course. Fifteen undergraduates took part, taking the vehicles from unboxing to custom autonomous racing algorithms and head-to-head track competition over just ten working days.

This high-intensity deployment exposed two critical hardware weaknesses that bench testing had missed:

1. **Power board thermal stress and current bottlenecks**: Sustained, multi-car racing pushed the initial power distribution board beyond its continuous current limits, causing thermal throttling and reliability issues. The board layout and heat sinking were immediately redesigned to handle heavy, continuous racing loads.
2. **Camera frame rate bottleneck (30 fps to 120 fps)**: The initial prototype used a 30 fps camera. At racing speeds exceeding 20 km/h (~6 m/s), the 33 ms inter-frame interval resulted in excessive physical displacement between frames, creating fatal latency for lane tracking and dynamic obstacle avoidance. The camera was upgraded to a 2.3 MP, 120 fps global-shutter sensor (dropping frame interval to 8.3 ms), eliminating perceptual lag during high-speed cornering.

These rapid hardware iterations were made possible only because students pushed the platform to its mechanical and algorithmic limits.

sections.heading: A global competition framework: From virtual qualifiers to track finals
sections.summary: Leveraging identical hardware specifications, the authors propose a league format modeled on FIRST Robotics and F1Tenth. Free browser simulation qualifiers feed into regional and international in-person races.
sections.details:
Because NeoRacer uses fixed, spec-locked hardware, competitions are decided purely by software intelligence rather than deep-pocketed mechanical upgrades. Building on this level playing field, the authors outline a tiered competition roadmap:

- **Virtual qualifiers**: Teams first compete in the browser-based Neobotics Playground simulator by submitting autonomous racing code to set lap times. Because it runs in any browser and requires no hardware or travel funding, any school worldwide can enter for free. Thanks to the shared API, qualifying code transfers directly to real vehicles.
- **Regional events and championships**: Student robotics clubs host local qualifiers using standardized track dimension guidelines and timing systems bundled into an open-source 'Host Kit'. Top regional finishers advance to an annual in-person championship featuring real-world autonomous wheel-to-wheel racing.
- **Aesthetic customization**: While performance-altering hardware modifications are strictly prohibited by technical regulations, teams are encouraged to customize 3D-printed body shells, liveries, and sponsor decals to showcase team identity without compromising racing fairness.

The rollout begins with an invitational exhibition race at IEEE VTC 2026 in Boston, scaling to collegiate regional circuits in 2027 and global championships across 2028 and 2029.

sections.heading: Sustainability and workforce development: Beyond a toy ecosystem
sections.summary: By training students on production-grade NVIDIA Orin and ROS2 architectures, NeoRacer builds industry-ready skills. A single-source partnership with Seeed Studio ensures a self-sustaining hardware supply chain independent of grants.
sections.details:
Many educational robotics kits simplify tools to the point of becoming toys, creating a wide skills gap between classroom learning and industrial practice. NeoRacer deliberately uses the exact same technology stack found across modern autonomous vehicle and commercial robotics companies: Jetson Orin compute, ROS2, CUDA, TensorRT, and CERN/GPL open-source licensing. Students master the workflows, optimization techniques, and middleware used in professional robotics careers.

To avoid the common pitfall where academic open-hardware projects die once research grant funding ends, manufacturing and global logistics are unified under Seeed Studio. Revenue from kit sales feeds directly into subsequent production runs, tooling maintenance, and software updates, creating a commercially viable, self-sustaining circular supply chain.

sections.heading: Open-source commitment: CERN-OHL-S v2 and GPLv3 licensing
sections.summary: Hardware schematics and mechanical assets are released under CERN-OHL-S v2, while software is licensed under GPLv3. Strong copyleft guarantees ensure that community improvements remain fully open.
sections.details:
All core NeoRacer assets are published under open-source licenses.

Hardware schematics and mechanical CAD files are governed by the CERN Open Hardware Licence Version 2, Strongly Reciprocal (CERN-OHL-S v2). This strong copyleft license requires that any downstream modifications or derivative hardware designs must also be shared openly under identical terms. The current release provides full schematics, wiring pinouts, and 3D CAD models for the OSCORE board, while full native EDA source files (including Gerber files) are being prepared for subsequent releases.

All software—including ROS2 driver wrappers, microcontroller firmware, and the Python racecar-neo-library—is licensed under the GNU General Public License v3 (GPLv3). Everything is publicly accessible and maintained on GitHub (https://github.com/Neobotics-Foundation-Inc/).

sections.heading: Conclusion: A new standard benchmark for autonomous racing
sections.summary: NeoRacer dismantles the long-standing barrier between costly research rigs and underpowered educational kits. Its unified hardware and open ecosystem establish a true standard benchmark for autonomous racing algorithms.
sections.details:
NeoRacer unites 67 TOPS of Jetson Orin Nano compute, wide-angle LiDAR, and a 120 fps global-shutter camera in a pre-assembled package priced around $2,700.

Refined through intense hands-on piloting at MIT to resolve real-world thermal and perceptual lag challenges, the platform is backed by the browser-based Playground simulator and a strict 3-identifier release tracking system. By removing hardware discrepancies from the equation, researchers and students can now compete and collaborate purely on algorithmic excellence, setting the stage for faster breakthroughs across autonomous racing, vehicle dynamics, and robotics education.

takeaways: Ensuring identical hardware and unified APIs across institutions is the single most critical factor for fair algorithm comparison and reproducibility in autonomous racing.
At racing speeds past 20 km/h, upgrading from 30 fps to a 120 fps global-shutter camera is essential to cut perception latency and keep high-speed controllers stable.
Physically isolating real-time control (actuator PWM, encoder decoding, fail-safes) on an ESP32 microcontroller prevents host Linux compute spikes from disrupting vehicle stability.

Pairing open-source designs with industrial manufacturing (Seeed Studio) and 3-identifier release tagging eliminates the hardware drift and batch inconsistencies that often derail open-hardware research.
limitations: While schematics and 3D CAD for the OSCORE board are public, raw PCB manufacturing Gerber and EDA project files have not yet been released in the current hardware revision (planned for the next update), limiting fully independent PCB fabrication.
Due to strict international air transport regulations, 3S LiPo drive batteries are not included in the standard shipping box and must be sourced locally by users.

The global competition circuit and standardized curriculum rollout are still in early stages; long-term multi-institution validation is currently limited to initial pilot deployments at MIT and Boston University.
